extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy (metaphysics/ethics); general educated readers
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and analytic criteria about personal identity (what makes the same person through time) and a taxonomy of relations (proportional, natural, instituted, moral), plus definitions of moral good/evil and kinds of law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal identity depends on consciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal identity is founded not on sameness of substance but on the same consciousness: 'it being the same consciousness that makes a man be himself to himself, personal identity depends on that only.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an intelligent being can repeat the idea of any past action with the same consciousness it had at first, and with the same consciousness it has of any present action, so far it is the same personal self. Examples include continuities across sleep, change of bodily substance, or time; the same consciousness unites distant actions into the same person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity is not identity of substance
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal identity is not determined by numerical identity of material or immaterial substance; different substances participating in the same consciousness can constitute one person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the composing substances change (material parts replaced, or different immaterial substances), personal identity may be preserved so long as the same consciousness continues. Analogies: different bodies united by one life make one animal; different substances united by one consciousness make one person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consciousness alone unites actions into the same Person
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing but consciousness can unite remote existences and actions into the same person; without consciousness there is no person, regardless of substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thought-experiments: one consciousness acting in two bodies yields one person in two bodies; two distinct consciousnesses acting in one body (day/night) yield two persons. Practical consequences: continuity of consciousness determines responsibility for past actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transferability of consciousness affects identity
rubrics_metrics.description: If the same consciousness could be transferred from one thinking substance to another, then those distinct thinking substances would constitute one person because personal identity follows the preserved consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke notes uncertainty about the nature of thinking substances and whether consciousness can be transferred; he allows the possibility in principle and invokes divine goodness to rule out unjust transfers that would affect reward/punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Same immaterial substance can make distinct persons if consciousness breaks
rubrics_metrics.description: The same immaterial soul or substance, if stripped of its past consciousness and unable to retrieve it, could ground a different person at a later time; continuity of consciousness, not sameness of soul, is decisive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a pre-existent spirit that has no recollection of past bodies would not be the same person as those earlier occupants (e.g., one cannot claim to be Socrates unless conscious of Socrates's actions).

rubrics_metrics.name: The body as well as the soul contributes to being the same man (man vs person distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Though personhood is determined by consciousness, the body contributes to what we call the same man; the same person and same man are often conflated in ordinary speech but conceptually distinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the prince's soul informing a cobbler's body would make that being the same person (in consciousness) as the prince for purposes of accountability, but others would regard him as the cobbler (the same man). Use this to separate forensic/personal identity from numerical human identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persons are the objects of reward and punishment (forensic criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: All right and justice of reward and punishment rest on personal identity as grounded in consciousness: happiness and misery are that for which a self (conscious being) is concerned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If consciousness accompanies certain past actions, the present self is justly accountable and may receive reward or punishment. Locke appeals to the idea that on the final judgment the consciousness of past deeds will be revealed and thus justify sentencing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolute oblivion separates forgotten actions from the person but not from the man
rubrics_metrics.description: If one wholly loses memory of parts of one's life beyond retrieval, those actions are for the purposes of personal identity not part of the current person, though the same man (biological individual) remains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal practice reflects this: the mad or the sober man are treated differently where consciousness differs; ordinary laws may still punish due to epistemic limits (drunkenness, sleepwalking) but strict moral reckoning depends on consciousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person is a forensic term
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'person' names the self insofar as it is conscious and capable of law, happiness, and misery; it is used to appropriate actions and their merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personhood extends beyond present existence to past actions only by consciousness: whatever past actions cannot be appropriated by present consciousness are not legitimately counted as belonged to that person for reward/punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportional relations (taxonomy of relations)
rubrics_metrics.description: One class of relations arises from comparing subjects by degrees or parts of a simple idea (e.g., whiter, sweeter, equal, more); these may be called proportional relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These relations depend on ideas received from sensation or reflection and are about equality or excess of the same simple idea across subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural relations (taxonomy of relations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural relations arise from circumstances of origin or beginning (e.g., father and son, brothers, countrymen) and are as lasting as the subjects because they depend on birth or origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Language and social practices mark these relations because of practical needs (laws, duties). Locke notes that in animals such relations exist but are often unnamed in language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instituted or voluntary relations (taxonomy of relations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instituted (voluntary) relations arise from acts by which someone acquires moral rights, powers, or obligations (e.g., a general and his army, a citizen with privileges).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These relations depend on human wills or agreements and are often alterable or separable from the substances involved; they are reciprocal but sometimes one side lacks a special relative name.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral relations (taxonomy and evaluative function)
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral relations consist in the conformity or disagreement of voluntary actions to some rule by which they are judged; they denominate moral actions and require careful definition to avoid confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral relations are central to evaluating actions as morally good or bad; Locke treats moral relations as mixed modes forming many of our ethical concepts (e.g., gratitude, polygamy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral good and evil defined as pleasure/pain and as conformity to law
rubrics_metrics.description: Good and evil are nothing but pleasure or pain (or that which procures them); moral good and evil are the conformity or disagreement of our voluntary actions to some law, whereby good or evil is drawn on us by the will and power of the law-maker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus moral evaluation depends both on consequences (pleasure/pain) and on the agent's relation to an enforcing law; rewards and punishments are the instruments by which law enforces moral rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three sorts of moral rules and laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The laws by which men judge their actions are three: (1) the Divine law (promulgated by nature or revelation), (2) the Civil law, and (3) the law of opinion or reputation; each determines whether actions are sins/duties, criminal/innocent, or virtues/vices respectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke emphasizes that a law requires an annexed enforcement (reward/punishment) beyond natural consequences; without such enforcement a rule would not function as a proper law governing free actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law requires extrinsic enforcement beyond natural consequence
rubrics_metrics.description: A law set to free actions must have some enforcement of good and evil (rewards/punishments) that are not the natural product of the action itself; otherwise the rule would be ineffectual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the 'true nature of all law properly so called' — law presupposes the power to reward or punish compliance or deviation in ways not automatically produced by the action's natural consequences.
